The tower measured 200 feet in length and 150 feet in
width, and was originally about 70 feet high. It was built
in four stages, a great solid mass of brickwork. Woolley
found an absence of straight lines. Horizontal planes bulged
outward, vertical planes were slightly convex-a subtlety
once thought to be of Greek origin and quite evident in the
Parthenon.
The lowest stage of the tower was black, the uppermost
red. The shrine was covered with blue glazed tile, the rqof
with gilded metal. Wooley writes, “These colors had mys-
tical significance and stood for the various divisions of the
universe, the dark underworld, the habitable earth, the
heavens and the sun.”
In another example, Herodotus in the fifth century B.C.
described what today are commonly known as Towers of
Babel to be found in Asia Minor. He wrote of battlements
and colors. To all indications Herodotus referred to the
great temple of Nebuchadnezzar which has been unearthed
in modern times. The architect James Fergusson wrote,

Here in America, the Navajos dwelt in a fabled land
surrounded by high mountains. These mountains rose and
fell to create day and night. The eastern mountains, as
might be expected, caused the day and were white. The
western mountains brought twilight and were yellow. The
northern mountains were black and covered the earth in
darkness. The southern mountains were blue and created
dawn and daylight.
Even today the Hopi Indian, in executing a sand painting,
may place a yellow color first for the north, then green or
blue for the west, red for the south, and white for the
east.
The Temple of Nebuchadnezzar, ca. 500 B.C.
The Earth
From heaven to earth, many primitive and ancient people
thought the world to be flat-and square. Even today,
travelers speak of making journeys to the four corners of the
earth. Color symbolism for the presumed four parts of the
earth is to be found in lands as far removed from each other
as China, India, Ireland, and Central and South America,
and among American Indians themselves. American Hopi Indian sand painting.

This theory of the elements prevailed for at least 20
centuries! In Greek symbolism, blue was for earth, green
for water, red for fire, and yellow for air.
The Jewish historian, Josephus, in the first century A.D.
related white with earth, purple with water, red with fire,
and yellow with air.
The ancient Chinese had five elements: yellow for earth,
black for water, red for fire, green for wood, and white for
metal.
The eminent Leonard0 da Vinci, in the 16th century A.D.
(nearly 20 centuries after the Greeks), set forth the doctrine

simple colors is white, though philosophers will not ac-
knowledge either white or black to be colors; because the

we shall place them among the others; and according to this
order of things, white will be the first, yellow the second,
green the third, blue the fourth, red the fifth, and black the
sixth. We shall set down white for the representative of light,
without which no color can be seen; yellow for the earth;
green for water; blue for air; red for fire; and black for total
darkness.”

During the Dark Ages, one of the greatest healers was
Avicenna, an Arabian. In his famous Canon of Medicine,
color was not only the sign of affliction-it might also be
the cure! First of all, the innate temperaments of men might
be found written in the color of their hair. People with black
hair had hot temperaments, while those with brown hair had
cold temperaments. The temperament of the tawny-headed
or red-headed person was equable. Here there was an excess
of “unburnt heat”; hence there was proneness to anger. The
temperament of the fair-haired was cold and very moist;
that of the gray-headed was cold and very dry. In both in-
stances Avicenna saw weakness and physical degeneracy.
Men, like plants, lost color as their years progressed.
Of humors he wrote: “Even imagination, emotional states
and other agents cause the humors to move. Thus, if one
were to gaze intently at something red, one would cause the
sanguineous humor to move. This is why one must not let
a person suffering from nosebleeding see things of a brilliant
red color.” l2 He also declared red and yellow to be injurious
to the eye. Blue light soothed the movement of the blood;
red light stimulated it. The clear light of morning aided
nutrition.
The healing properties of color still fascinate some
mystics and some charlatans. One master here of the last
century, Edwin D. Babbitt, claimed to cure just about every
ailment known to man with color. And he has had followers
and avatars who still attempt to practice such supposedly
therapeutic legerdemain.
In Babbitt’s concept of color and healing, red was the
warming element of sunlight. It was presumed to have a
rousing, effect upon the blood and to be therapeutic in pa-
ralysis and dormant chronic conditions. Plate from Edwin D. Babbitt’s work on color healing.
Yellow and orange stimulated the nerves. They were
supposed to be good as a laxative and for those suffering
from bronchial difficulties.

Epilogue
The world today, sophisticated as it is, may be quite aware
of the nature of color. With modern scientific instruments,
elaborate color production and reproduction methods, the
laser, colorimeters and spectrophotometers, behind all this
current knowledge lies an innate attraction to the spectrum,
a natural and man-made phenomenon that never fails to
arouse deepset human responses.
